models.name: SCNet-large
models.developer: starrytong (paper authors); distributed via ZFTurbo Music-Source-Separation-Training
models.summary: Frequency-domain Sparse Compression Network for 4-stem music source separation (vocals/drums/bass/other). The 'large' variant is a high-SDR upgrade over the base model and is one of the strongest single models for bass and drum stems specifically. In an independent ensemble study, SCNet-large was the top-selected model for bass (67% of cases) and drums (93%), making it the go-to for clean rhythm-section stems. It is light: the architecture family is ~10M params with CPU inference at ~48% of HT Demucs time, so on a 5090 it runs near-instant with a tiny VRAM footprint. Original weights are MIT; it is fully supported in the ZFTurbo MSST toolkit for both inference and LoRA-style fine-tuning.
models.params: ~10M (base); large variant larger but still small-model class
models.commercial_notes: Both the original starrytong/SCNet repo and the ZFTurbo MSST distribution framework are MIT-licensed, including the released checkpoints. Commercial use is permitted; attribution per MIT. Pretrained weights trained on MUSDB18-HQ.
models.speed_note: Very fast — CPU inference ~48% of HT Demucs; near-real-time on a 5090 with minimal VRAM. Inference is light; the A6000-48GB note in MSST refers to training batch sizes, not inference.

best_for.purpose: Multi-stem separation (vocals/drums/bass/other)
Game-audio stem prep (isolating drums/bass/melody for adaptive layering)
Dataset cleanup (extracting clean stems / removing music or vocals from source audio)
Bass and drum stem isolation specifically (its strongest categories)

models.name: SCNet-XL
models.summary: The top-of-line SCNet variant, released in the ZFTurbo MSST framework (v1.0.13). Pushes 4-stem separation quality to the current open-weight frontier: MUSDB test SDR avg 9.80 (SCNet-XL) and 10.08 for the XL-IHF tuning — among the highest reported for any single open model, ahead of HT Demucs. Same MIT licensing and ComfyUI-compatible workflow story as SCNet-large; the trade-off is a larger checkpoint and slower inference than base/large, but still comfortably within a 5090's envelope. Pick this when separation quality matters more than throughput.

models.name: Ultimate Vocal Remover 5 (UVR5)
models.summary: The de-facto end-user front-end for music source separation — a standalone GUI app (Windows/macOS/Linux), not a model or library. It wraps multiple separation backends (Demucs v3/v4 4-stem, MDX-Net, VR Architecture, MDX23C) behind a point-and-click interface with a model download manager, batch processing, and ensemble modes. This is the practical tool for non-coders to do vocal isolation, instrumental extraction, de-reverb/de-echo, and 4-stem splits without touching Python. Hardware needs are tiny (GTX 1060 6GB min, 8GB VRAM recommended) so a 5090 is wildly overpowered. The GUI is MIT-licensed; commercial use of OUTPUTS depends on the specific model selected, since each bundled checkpoint carries its own terms.
models.base_arch: GUI front-end wrapping Demucs / MDX-Net / VR Arch / MDX23C
models.commercial_notes: The UVR5 GUI itself is MIT-licensed (attribution requested). However it is a front-end: commercial use of separated audio depends on the LICENSE of whichever model you run through it. The UVR-trained models and Demucs (also MIT) are generally permissive, but each model's terms govern its outputs — verify per model before commercial release. Treat the app as MIT, the weights case-by-case.
models.speed_note: Trivial on a 5090 (min spec is a GTX 1060 6GB). GPU-accelerated; throughput is gated by the chosen model, not the hardware. Windows install must go to the C:\ drive per the installer.

research.notes:
WAVE 4 audio tail — 3 entries added (target 2-4). Two SCNet model entries + the UVR5 front-end, per lane brief. Did NOT re-list the 9 already-cataloged audio models. KEY FINDINGS / DECISIONS:
1. LICENSE (decisive axis) — all three are MIT and commercial-safe at the code level. SCNet original (starrytong/SCNet) = MIT; ZFTurbo MSST distribution framework = MIT; UVR5 GUI = MIT. All SCNet checkpoints trained on MUSDB18-HQ and released under the same MIT terms. 2. UVR5 commercial_use set to 'conditional' (not 'yes') ON PURPOSE: per the lane brief's instruction to set commercial_use/license correctly for a GUI front-end. The APP is MIT, but it is a wrapper — commercial use of separated OUTPUT depends on the specific model checkpoint loaded (Demucs=MIT/permissive; UVR-trained models permissive; but each model's terms govern). Flagged this explicitly in commercial_notes. 3. VRAM / 32GB filter — all three pass with huge headroom. SCNet is a small-model-class architecture (~10M params, CPU inference ~48% of HT Demucs). IMPORTANT: the 'A6000 48GB' figure in the MSST repo is for TRAINING batch sizes, not inference — I did NOT mislabel that as a VRAM requirement. UVR5 min spec is a GTX 1060 6GB. A 5090 (32GB) runs all of these trivially. 4. ADDED genuinely-new sibling: SCNet-XL (status runner-up). It's the highest-SDR variant (MUSDB avg 9.80; XL-IHF 10.08), released in MSST v1.0.13, and clearly distinct from SCNet-large (avg 9.32). Justified by the brief's 'plus a genuinely-new sibling if obvious' clause. 5. SCNet-large strength is bass+drums specifically — independent ensemble study (arXiv 2410.20773) found it selected as best-for-bass in 67% and best-for-drums in 93% of cases. Directly relevant to game-audio stem prep (isolating rhythm-section layers for adaptive soundtracks). 6. MVSep NOTE — the lane brief paired 'MVSep / UVR5' as the leading end-user front-ends. I cataloged UVR5 (locally-installable desktop app, fits the 32GB-local catalog). MVSep (mvsep.com) is primarily a HOSTED WEB SERVICE / cloud separation site, not a local model or installable app, so it does NOT fit a local-AI / 32GB-VRAM catalog and was deliberately NOT given its own entry. If a cloud-service entry is desired it can be noted separately, but it falls outside the local-rig scope. All facts verified live via WebSearch + WebFetch on 2026-06-02 against official HF/GitHub cards and the source paper.

research.notes: WAVE 4 narrow tail — alibaba-pai VideoX-Fun control line, camera-trajectory branch. All four cataloged models are Apache-2.0 (fully commercial-safe, no gated terms, no Wan-specific extra clause — the alibaba-pai Fun fine-tunes carry Apache-2.0, NOT the more restrictive base-Wan terms; QuantStack GGUFs inherit Apache-2.0). License is the decisive axis here and it lands clean: all four are commercial-OK and LoRA-trainable. Both A14B models are Wan 2.2 MoE (dual high-noise + low-noise expert) — native fp16 is 64 GB and does NOT fit a 32 GB card without GGUF or aggressive cpu_offload; the QuantStack GGUF repos are the actual 32 GB fit and are the load-bearing extras for this rig. Because the A14B is MoE, the GGUF repos ship HighNoise/ + LowNoise/ subfolders (confirmed on the file tree); the per-file sizes reported by some card summaries (~10–16 GB) are PER EXPERT — real ComfyUI usage loads both, so budget ~2× at full residency, but ComfyUI's native Wan 2.2 sampler streams experts sequentially so Q4–Q5 fits 32 GB comfortably and Q8 is borderline-OK. The dense 5B siblings (Wan2.2-Fun-5B-Control / -Control-Camera, 23 GB native, ~10 GB at Q4 GGUF) are the trivially-safe fit and are noted as best-fit alternatives, but the A14B pair + their GGUFs are the substantive catalog entries the lane targets. ComfyUI support is first-party via VideoX-Fun (github.com/aigc-apps/VideoX-Fun, comfyui/ dir) and community via city96 ComfyUI-GGUF + Kijai nodes. Camera model = pure trajectory conditioning (pan U/D/L/R, zoom in/out, combined moves) — exactly the cutscene/marketing camera-move use the lane asks for. The plain Control model is distinct: multi-modal structural control (Canny/Depth/Pose/MLSD + trajectory + reference image), kept as a separate entry per the "if distinct" instruction. Collection updated 2025-10-09; current as of 2026-06-02. Did NOT re-catalog the already-covered Wan 2.2 base/Animate/TI2V-5B/Fun-A14B-Control(base)/S2V/VACE-Fun — these are the remaining camera + multi-control siblings only.

The QuantStack GGUF repos' claimed HighNoise/ + LowNoise/ dual-expert MoE folder structure is CONFIRMED via the file tree (each folder ~13 files), and the per-expert quant sizes in the claims match the on-page tables exactly (Camera Q4_K_M 10.7 GB / Q8_0 16.4 GB; Control Q4_K_M 9.66 GB / Q8_0 15.4 GB plus Q2_K 6.32 GB for the camera variant — note the claim's "6.32 Q2_K" is actually the camera repo's value; the multi-control repo's Q2_K is 5.31 GB). research.notes: WAVE 4 narrow tail — FLUX.2 klein quantized + non-distilled base variants. Added 4 formal rows; all confirmed live via HF cards + file trees on 2026-06-02. KEY STRUCTURAL FINDING (changes the picture vs the lane brief): The klein family has TWO axes, not one. (a) distilled vs NON-DISTILLED "base" — the "base" line is a genuinely distinct release (separate repos: FLUX.2-klein-base-4B / -base-9B), explicitly the undistilled full-capacity foundation models 'preserving complete training signal,' positioned by BFL for fine-tuning/LoRA. (b) precision: BF16 / FP8 / NVFP4 official quants exist for the distilled line, and FP8 quants also exist for the base line (e.g. klein-base-4b-fp8, klein-base-9b-fp8) plus a KV-cache variant family (klein-9b-kv). I did not give every quant its own row in a narrow tail; I picked the strategically distinct ones. LICENSE AXIS (decisive for this rig): The split is clean and confirmed on every card — - ALL 4B variants (base, distilled, fp8, nvfp4) = Apache 2.0 → commercial-safe, LoRA-trainable. GREEN for game-asset + marketing. - ALL 9B variants (base, distilled, fp8, kv) = FLUX Non-Commercial License → blocked for the rig's commercial mandate. RED. ROW SELECTION RATIONALE: 1. klein-base-4B (RECOMMENDED) — the headline add. Only commercial-safe + non-distilled + LoRA-trainable FLUX.2 base, ~13 GB VRAM. Distinct from the already-cataloged distilled 4B (which is Apache but distilled => not the right training base). This is the single most valuable klein-family entry for the rig's game-asset use case. 2. klein-4B-FP8 (situational) — Apache, 4.07 GB, fast commercial inference / marketing. 3. klein-4B-NVFP4 (situational) — Apache, 2.46 GB, RTX 5090 Blackwell FP4-native => fastest klein path on THIS exact rig. Quality 'strong' (4-bit) not 'frontier'. 4. klein-base-9B (legacy FOR THIS USE CASE) — distinct non-distilled 9B base the brief asked to confirm; FLUX Non-Commercial so OUT for commercial work despite frontier quality. Fits ~29 GB (tight on 32 GB). Folded its FP8 sibling (klein-9b-fp8, 9.43 GB, same non-commercial license) into notes rather than a separate row. VRAM/DISK confirmed from file trees (not just card claims): base-4B ~8.4 GB on disk (folder-format diffusers repo) / ~13 GB VRAM; 4b-fp8 4.07 GB; 4b-nvfp4 2.46 GB; base-9B 18.2 GB single safetensors / ~29 GB VRAM; 9b-fp8 9.43 GB. All fit on 32 GB; only the 9B line is tight. DID NOT re-catalog (already covered): distilled klein 4B (Apache), distilled klein 9B (non-commercial), FLUX.2 [dev], Qwen-Image. Quants/siblings deliberately omitted to honor narrow-tail scope: klein-base-4b-fp8, klein-base-4b-nvfp4, klein-base-9b-fp8, klein-9b-kv / klein-9b-kv-fp8 (KV-cache editing variants), and third-party GGUFs (unsloth/leejet) — all exist and are live, none change the license verdict per axis.

Companion to Impact Pack (same author).
